newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian sugar industry demands price deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Indian sugar industry demands price deregulation.

text.p: India's sugar industry called on Friday for deregulation of sugar prices to minimise fluctuations in output and reduce losses on exports.

"If we have to be competitive in the world market, I for one cannot fathom any other solution except the decontrol of sugar (prices) on a long-term basis," said Vivek Saraogi, president of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA).
Saraogi was speaking at the annual general meeting of ISMA, the top organisation of Indian sugar mills.
Production and pricing of sugar in India are controlled by the government.

The mills supply 40 percent of their output as levy at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor. The government controls the release of the remainder on the free market through the use of sales quotas.
Industry officials say under the current rules the industry is forced to supply sugar to the poor at prices which are set by the government and are often below the cost of production.
Sugar mill owners want to supply 20 percent instead of 40 percent of their output as a levy for distribution among poor.

"Our principal handicap is the dual pricing policy which artificially pushes up the cost of exported sugar. No other sugar exporting country with whom we compete suffers from this handicap," Saraogi said.
India has abolished licenses for many industries as part of sweeping economic reforms launched in 1991. But it has maintained a grip over the sugar industry.
In August the government ended a monopoly held by private company, set up by the sugar millers, over exports.
Saraogi said deregulation of sugar prices would enhance efficiency, minimise fluctuations in production and facilitate a greater volume of exports at competitive prices.

On Thursday, the ISMA said India's sugar output in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) rose to a record 16.4 million tonnes, up from last year's 14.6 million. India consumes about 13 million tonnes of sugar every year.
ISMA has projected an output of 16 million tonnes in 1996/97.
The sugar industry exported nearly one million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96.
Saraogi said currently the projected loss on the export of one tonne of sugar was about 1,450 rupees, or $40.

"In the event of a decontrol, the projected loss on the export of one million tonnes of sugar would have been considerably reduced to only a fifth of the estimated loss involved under the present policy," he said.
